title: Kohlhaas v. State
description: Whether Alaska's Initiative 2, which established a nonpartisan open primary and ranked-choice voting, violates the Alaska Constitution by infringing on political parties' associational rights, altering the method for electing the lieutenant governor, and conflicting with the plurality requirement for electing the governor.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Initiative 2 violated political parties' associational rights by diminishing their control over candidate selection and forcing unwanted association, violated the Alaska Constitution's provision for electing the lieutenant governor by pairing candidates in the primary, and unconstitutionally burdened the right to vote by requiring a majority for the governor and denying victory to the candidate with the greatest number of first-choice votes.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that Initiative 2 does not violate associational rights because it decouples the state's election system from party nominations, that the lieutenant governor election provisions are constitutional as the law allows flexibility, and that ranked-choice voting does not require a majority to win and does not unconstitutionally burden the right to vote.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's judgment, upholding the constitutionality of Alaska's Initiative 2, which implemented a nonpartisan open primary and ranked-choice voting.

title: State Department of Education & Early Development v. Alexander
description: Whether Alaska statutes permitting public funds for correspondence study programs, which can be used for private school tuition, violate the state constitution's prohibition against direct benefits to religious or other private educational institutions.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (Alexander) argued that the statutes allowing public funds for correspondence study, particularly for private school tuition, are facially unconstitutional or unconstitutional as applied, violating the state constitution's prohibition against direct benefits to private educational institutions.
defendant_argument: The defendant (State Department of Education) argued that the statutes are facially constitutional because they have a "plainly legitimate sweep" with many valid uses of funds, even if some applications (like private school tuition) might be unconstitutional. Intervenor-appellants (Moceri) argued that the benefit to private schools is indirect and thus permissible.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the superior court's judgment, ruling that the allotment and ILP statutes are not facially unconstitutional and remanding the case for further proceedings, declining to rule on the constitutionality of using funds for private school tuition at this stage.

title: Valoaga v. State
description: Whether the Department of Corrections (DOC) violated an inmate's due process rights by using a preponderance of the evidence standard in disciplinary proceedings and by not offering an alternative saliva test for drug screening.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that DOC must prove prison rule violations by clear and convincing evidence, not a preponderance of the evidence, and that failing to offer a saliva test when he could not urinate violated his due process rights.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the Alaska Constitution permits the use of a preponderance of the evidence standard in prison disciplinary proceedings and that the plaintiff's argument regarding saliva tests was not preserved for review.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's decision, ruling that the preponderance of the evidence standard is constitutional for prison disciplinary proceedings and that the argument regarding alternative saliva tests was waived.

title: Alaska Trappers Association v. City of Valdez
description: Whether a city ordinance limiting trapping in certain areas is preempted by state law, with the plaintiff arguing it is preempted by state authority over natural resources, and the defendant arguing it is a valid exercise of local home rule authority for public safety and land use.
plaintiff_argument: The city's ordinance limiting trapping is preempted by state law, violates AS 16.05.790, and article VIII of the Alaska Constitution, as the state has pervasive authority over natural resources and the Board of Game has sole authority over trapping.
defendant_argument: The city has constitutional and statutory authority as a home rule municipality to regulate land use and public safety, and its ordinance is not expressly or impliedly prohibited by state law, as its impact on wildlife management is incidental.
decision_outcome: The superior court's order granting summary judgment to the City of Valdez was affirmed, concluding that the city's ordinance is not prohibited by the Alaska Constitution or the legislature's delegation of authority over fish and game to the Board.

title: State v. McKelvey
description: Whether police must obtain a warrant before taking pictures of a person's yard with a zoom lens from an airplane, with the State arguing it is permissible due to common air travel and public visibility, and the respondent arguing it constitutes an unreasonable search under the Alaska Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that because small airplane travel is common in Alaska and any passenger might peer into a yard, law enforcement officials may do the same without a warrant.
defendant_argument: McKelvey argued that the warrantless observation of his home with a telephoto lens during a flight constituted an illegal search under the Alaska Constitution.
decision_outcome: The Alaska Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that law enforcement officials must obtain a warrant before using aircraft and vision-enhancing technology to observe the curtilage of a person's home that is protected from ground-level observation.

title: Vazquez v. State
description: Whether Jennie Armstrong met the constitutional three-year Alaska residency requirement to be eligible to serve in the legislature.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that Armstrong did not establish Alaska residency until June 7, 2019, at the earliest, making her ineligible for the 2022 election.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that Armstrong established Alaska residency on May 20, 2019, thereby meeting the three-year residency requirement for the 2022 election.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's conclusion that Jennie Armstrong is eligible to serve in the legislature, finding she established residency on May 20, 2019.

title: Native Village of Kwinhagak v. State, Department of Health & Social Services
description: Whether the Office of Children's Services (OCS) must follow civil commitment statutes when admitting a child in its custody to a hospital for psychiatric treatment, and whether a 46-day hospitalization without a prompt hearing violates the child's constitutional due process rights.
plaintiff_argument: The Native Village of Kwinhagak argued that OCS must follow civil commitment statutes for psychiatric hospitalization and that the prolonged hospitalization without a prompt hearing violated the child's constitutional due process rights.
defendant_argument: The State of Alaska argued that OCS has authority under CINA statutes to admit children to psychiatric care, not civil commitment statutes, and that existing injunctions provided sufficient procedural protections.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the superior court's order, ruling that OCS was not required to follow civil commitment statutes for psychiatric hospitalization but that the 46-day delay in holding a hearing violated the child's procedural due process rights.

title: Sitka Tribe of Alaska v. State
description: Whether the State of Alaska has a constitutional duty to provide all relevant information to the Board of Fisheries for natural resource management, whether the Sitka Tribe of Alaska demonstrated irreparable harm for a preliminary injunction, and whether the Tribe was the prevailing party for attorney's fees.
plaintiff_argument: The Sitka Tribe of Alaska argued that the Alaska Constitution requires the Department to provide all relevant information to the Board, that they faced irreparable harm warranting a preliminary injunction, and that they were the prevailing party entitled to attorney's fees.
defendant_argument: The State and the Alliance argued that there is no constitutional duty to provide all relevant information, that the Tribe did not face irreparable harm, and that the Tribe was not the prevailing party for attorney's fees.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the superior court's decisions, denying the Tribe's constitutional claim, finding no irreparable harm for a preliminary injunction, and denying attorney's fees to all parties.

title: Taylor v. Alaska Legislative Affairs Agency
description: Whether the Alaska Constitution bars a lawsuit brought by the Attorney General against the Legislative Affairs Agency, with the plaintiff arguing it is not barred due to common law authority and the ability to challenge non-legislative acts, and the defendant arguing it is barred by Article III, Section 16, as an action against the legislature.
plaintiff_argument: Attorney General Taylor argued that his suit was not barred by the Alaska Constitution, asserting common law authority to sue on the State's behalf distinct from the governor's constitutional authority, and that prior precedent (Knowles) allowed him to challenge non-legislative acts of the Legislative Affairs Agency.
defendant_argument: The Legislative Affairs Agency argued that the suit was constitutionally barred by Article III, Section 16 of the Alaska Constitution, as it was an action brought "in the name of the State" and "against the legislature," and that the Attorney General's authority in this context is substantively the same as the governor's.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's decision, granting summary judgment to the Legislative Affairs Agency and dismissing the Attorney General's lawsuit as unconstitutional under Article III, Section 16 of the Alaska Constitution, while vacating and remanding the attorney's fees award for further proceedings.

title: Williams Alaska Petroleum, Inc. v. State
description: Whether Williams Alaska Petroleum, Inc. is strictly liable for sulfolane and PFAS contamination, associated damages, and remediation costs, and whether the superior court's decision violated Williams's due process rights or constituted an unconstitutional taking.
plaintiff_argument: The State and Flint Hills argued that Williams is strictly liable for sulfolane and PFAS releases, that sulfolane is a hazardous substance, and that Williams must pay damages, response costs, and contribute to remediation.
defendant_argument: Williams argued that sulfolane is not a hazardous substance, that the awarded damages and costs were erroneous, that the injunctive and declaratory relief was improper, that the purchase agreement was misinterpreted regarding liability allocation, and that the decision violated due process and constituted an unconstitutional taking.
decision_outcome: The court largely affirmed the superior court's decision, concluding that Williams is strictly liable for sulfolane and PFAS releases, awarding response costs and natural resource damages to the State and Flint Hills, and affirming contribution awards, but remanded the injunctive relief for more specificity.

title: In re Abigail B.
description: Whether the lengthy pre-evaluation detentions of individuals for mental health evaluations, due to lack of facility capacity, violate their substantive due process rights, with plaintiffs arguing such detentions are not reasonably related to the purpose of immediate transport for evaluation, and the defendant arguing for broader purposes for detention.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that their prolonged pre-evaluation detentions violated their substantive due process rights because the nature and duration of these detentions were not reasonably related to the purpose of facilitating immediate transportation for evaluation. They also proposed a seven-day presumptive violation and sanctions for the State.
defendant_argument: The State argued that pre-evaluation detentions serve broader purposes, including protecting individuals and society and providing treatment, and that the detentions were reasonably related to these broader purposes. The State opposed a seven-day presumption and court-imposed sanctions.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the superior court orders that authorized the continued pre-evaluation detention of Abigail B. and Jethro S., finding that their substantive due process rights were violated.

title: In re 2021 Redistricting Cases
description: Whether the Alaska Redistricting Board's legislative redistricting plans for House and Senate districts comply with constitutional requirements, specifically regarding unconstitutional political gerrymandering and equal protection.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Board's plans, including Senate District K, amended Senate Districts E and L, and the Cantwell Appendage in House District 36, were unconstitutional due to political gerrymandering, equal protection violations, and failures to meet compactness and socioeconomic integration requirements.
defendant_argument: The defendant (Alaska Redistricting Board) argued that its redistricting plans complied with constitutional requirements for compactness, socioeconomic integration, and equal protection, and that the Board followed proper procedures.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed that the Board's Senate District K and the amended Senate Districts E and L constituted unconstitutional political gerrymandering, found the 'Cantwell Appendage' in House District 36 unconstitutional for lack of compactness, and ordered the adoption of an interim redistricting plan while remanding for a final constitutional plan.

title: Knolmayer v. McCollum
description: Whether Alaska Statute 09.55.548(b), which limits the recovery of damages compensated by collateral sources, violates the equal protection guarantee of the Alaska Constitution when applied to a medical malpractice claimant whose insurer has a contractual right to reimbursement.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that AS 09.55.548(b) violates equal protection by creating an unfair distinction between different types of medical malpractice claimants, leading to a 'double deduction' and forcing them to bear the loss, which is contrary to legislative intent.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that AS 09.55.548(b) is a legislative policy choice to reduce damages awards and that its classifications are subject to minimum scrutiny, bearing a fair and substantial relation to the legitimate government objective of eliminating double recoveries.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the superior court's order and remanded the case, concluding that AS 09.55.548(b)'s limitation on recovery of collateral source compensation violates Alaska's equal protection clause when applied to a claimant who receives compensation from a collateral source that exercises a right of reimbursement against the claimant's recovery.

title: Short v. State
description: Whether the Higher Education Investment Fund (HEIF) is subject to the state's annual budgetary "sweep" into the Constitutional Budget Reserve, with students arguing it is not sweepable and the Executive Branch arguing it is.
plaintiff_argument: The students argued that the HEIF is not sweepable because its appropriations do not lapse, it has already been validly appropriated and expended for investments, and sweeping it would violate separation of powers. They also contended that the precedent of Cowper should be overruled.
defendant_argument: The Executive Branch argued that the HEIF is sweepable under Hickel v. Cowper precedent because it is in the general fund and requires further legislative appropriation before expenditure. They maintained that the sweep does not violate separation of powers and Cowper should not be overruled.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the superior court's decision that the Higher Education Investment Fund (HEIF) is sweepable under the state's constitutional budgetary "sweep" provision.

title: Department of Corrections v. Stefano
description: Whether the superior court has appellate jurisdiction to review the Department of Corrections' (DOC) decision to remove an inmate from electronic monitoring, and whether DOC's decision implicates the inmate's constitutional rights to due process and rehabilitation.
plaintiff_argument: Stefano argued that his removal from electronic monitoring violated his constitutional rights to due process and rehabilitation, and that the superior court had appellate jurisdiction to review DOC's decision because it involved fundamental constitutional rights and an adjudicative record.
defendant_argument: The Department of Corrections (DOC) argued that the superior court lacked appellate jurisdiction to review its decision, that electronic monitoring is not a formal rehabilitative program, and that its decision to remove Stefano did not implicate a fundamental constitutional right to rehabilitation or produce an adjudicative record for review.
decision_outcome: The court held that serving a sentence on electronic monitoring affords a limited but constitutionally protected degree of liberty, requiring due process for removal. However, the court also held that the superior court lacked appellate jurisdiction to review DOC's decision in this case because DOC's decisional process was not an adjudicative proceeding and did not create an adequate record for appellate review. The court vacated the superior court's decision and remanded the case to be converted into a civil action for judicial review.

title: State v. The Alaska Legislative Council
description: Whether the Alaska Legislature's practice of "forward funding" public education, which appropriates funds for two consecutive fiscal years, is consistent with the annual budgeting process established by the Alaska Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Legislative Council and Coalition for Education Equity argued that forward-funded appropriations were constitutional, did not violate any specific constitutional provision, and the governor's refusal to disburse funds violated his duty to faithfully execute the laws.
defendant_argument: The State of Alaska (Governor Dunleavy) argued that forward funding violated the annual appropriations model established by the Alaska Constitution, infringing on the governor's veto power and the prohibition on dedicating revenues.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the superior court's decision, ruling that the forward-funded appropriations are unconstitutional because they are inconsistent with the annual budgeting process implied by the Alaska Constitution.

title: State v. Graham
description: Whether the Court of Appeals erred in vacating Stacey Graham's sentence and remanding for resentencing before a different judge, specifically regarding the application of sentencing standards and the admissibility of victim impact evidence.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the superior court properly applied sentencing standards and that the admission of police testimony and victim tribute videos did not warrant vacating the sentence or requiring a different judge for resentencing.
defendant_argument: Graham argued his sentence was excessive due to errors in applying sentencing benchmarks, improper reliance on aggravating factors, and the improper admission of emotionally charged victim impact evidence (police testimony and tribute videos), which necessitated resentencing by a different judge.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, vacated Graham's sentence, and remanded for resentencing by the same judge, finding errors in the admission of police officer testimony and victim tribute videos (without prior review) but no errors in the sentencing standards applied by the superior court or the need for judge recusal.

title: Association of Village Council Presidents Regional Housing Authority v. Mael
description: Whether the housing authority owed a tort duty to inspect the boiler, whether that duty was in effect at the time of the explosion, and whether the statutory damages cap was correctly applied to Dietrich Mael's and his family members' noneconomic damages.
plaintiff_argument: The housing authority had a tort duty to inspect the boiler, which it negligently violated, causing injuries, and the statutory damages cap should not apply to Dietrich's severe injuries or be aggregated with his family's distinct emotional distress claims.
defendant_argument: The housing authority's duty to inspect was contractual and had expired, the boiler explosion was due to a product defect, not negligence, and all noneconomic damages, including family members' emotional distress, should be subject to a single statutory cap.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's judgment, upholding that the housing authority had a tort duty to inspect the boiler, that its negligence caused the explosion, and that Dietrich's noneconomic damages were capped at $1 million while his family members' emotional distress damages were subject to separate caps.

title: Dutchess v. Dutch
description: Whether the superior court erred in granting the father sole legal custody to make vaccination decisions for their minor children, despite the mother's religious objections and claims of constitutional violations.
plaintiff_argument: The mother argued that granting the father sole legal custody for vaccination decisions infringed upon her constitutional right to free exercise of religion and violated her due process rights.
defendant_argument: The father argued that vaccinating the children was in their best interests, as recommended by their pediatrician, and sought sole legal custody for vaccination decisions.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's order, granting the father sole legal authority to make vaccination decisions for the children.

title: Sagoonick v. State
description: Whether the State of Alaska's resource development policies, which contribute to climate change, violate the constitutional rights of young Alaskans, or if such claims are non-justiciable political questions for the legislative and executive branches.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the State's resource development policies contribute to climate change, violating their fundamental constitutional rights to a stable climate system, life, liberty, property, and equal protection, and breaching the public trust doctrine.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the plaintiffs' claims presented non-justiciable political questions, better left to the legislative and executive branches, and that the judiciary's role in natural resource policy is limited to ensuring constitutional principles are followed, not making policy judgments.
decision_outcome: The Alaska Supreme Court affirmed the superior court's dismissal of the plaintiffs' lawsuit, concluding that the injunctive relief claims were non-justiciable political questions and the declaratory relief claims were properly dismissed on prudential grounds.

title: Department of Administration v. Retired Public Employees of Alaska, Inc.
description: Whether the 2014 redesign of the dental insurance plan for retirees unconstitutionally diminished accrued benefits, and whether premium rates should be considered in the diminishment analysis.
plaintiff_argument: The 2014 plan unconstitutionally diminished retirees' accrued benefits by narrowing coverage, and the premiums paid by retirees are irrelevant to the diminishment analysis.
defendant_argument: Dental coverage for public retirees is not an "accrued benefit" protected by the Alaska Constitution, or if it is, changes in premium rates paid by enrollees must be considered in the diminishment analysis.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the superior court's judgment and remanded the case for a new diminishment analysis that incorporates premium pricing, agreeing that the option to purchase dental insurance is an accrued benefit but disagreeing that premiums are irrelevant.

title: Dunleavy v. Alaska Legislative Council ex rel. Alaska State Legislature
description: Whether legislative inaction on gubernatorial appointments, as defined by statute, is equivalent to a denial of confirmation, or if appointees remain in office until the legislature affirmatively votes on their confirmation.
plaintiff_argument: The Legislative Council argued that legislative inaction on gubernatorial appointments, as defined by statute, is tantamount to a denial of confirmation, meaning those appointees cannot continue to serve.
defendant_argument: The Governor argued that his appointees remain in office until the legislature affirmatively votes to confirm or reject them, and that laws defining inaction as rejection are unconstitutional.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the superior court's judgment, ruling that the statutes defining legislative inaction as a denial of confirmation violate the Alaska Constitution.

title: State v. Arctic Village Council
description: Whether the absentee ballot witness requirement unconstitutionally burdened the right to vote during the COVID-19 pandemic.
plaintiff_argument: The witness requirement forced voters, especially vulnerable ones, to risk their health to vote or forgo voting, thus unconstitutionally burdening their fundamental right to vote during the pandemic.
defendant_argument: The witness requirement was necessary to deter fraud and promote voter confidence, and the plaintiffs unreasonably delayed in bringing the suit, making their claims barred by laches.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's decision to grant a preliminary injunction, suspending the absentee ballot witness requirement for the 2020 general election.

title: State v. Recall Dunleavy
description: Whether the recall application against Governor Dunleavy, citing lack of fitness, incompetence, and neglect of duties, was legally and factually sufficient to proceed to a special election.
plaintiff_argument: The Recall Dunleavy committee argued that their application, detailing specific actions by the governor, was legally and factually sufficient to warrant a recall election.
defendant_argument: The State of Alaska, Office of Lieutenant Governor, Division of Elections and Director Gail Fenumiai, argued that the recall application was not legally or factually sufficient.
decision_outcome: The Alaska Supreme Court affirmed the superior court's decision, ruling that the recall application, with the exception of one subpart, satisfied the legal requirements for presentation to the voters.

title: State v. Galvin
description: Whether the Division of Elections' ballot design, which omitted a candidate's nonpartisan voter registration, violated statutory requirements and the candidate's right to free political association under the Alaska Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Alyse Galvin argued that the Division of Elections' ballot design, which omitted her nonpartisan voter registration, violated a statutory directive to designate a candidate's party affiliation on the ballot and her right to free political association.
defendant_argument: The Division of Elections argued that its ballot design was permissible, that 'party affiliation' and 'party designation' were synonymous, and that granting a preliminary injunction to change the ballots would jeopardize the prospects of a successful and timely election.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the superior court's denial of Alyse Galvin's requested preliminary injunction, ruling that granting it would imperil the public interest in an orderly and timely election.

title: Watson v. State
description: Whether the Alaska statute that excludes misdemeanor traffic violations from juvenile court jurisdiction, thereby requiring minors accused of such offenses to be prosecuted as adults, violates the right to equal protection under the Alaska Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Watson argued that the statute violates her equal protection rights because it unfairly treats minors accused of misdemeanor DUI as adults with mandatory jail sentences, while allowing minors accused of felony DUI to be tried in juvenile court, and that this differential treatment is unfair compared to other misdemeanors in the juvenile code.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the statute is constitutional because driving is an adult activity, and the legislature can reasonably treat misdemeanor traffic violations uniformly to promote public safety, while also protecting juvenile offenders from the severe collateral consequences of felony convictions.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that the statute is constitutional and affirmed the judgment of the district court, ruling against Watson's equal protection claim.

title: Metcalfe v. State
description: Whether the repeal of a statutory provision allowing former state employees to reinstate their credited service and original benefits tier upon re-employment and repayment of withdrawn contributions diminished or impaired an accrued benefit of the retirement system, protected by Article XII, Section 7 of the Alaska Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the statutory right to reinstate credited service was an accrued benefit protected by Article XII, Section 7 of the Alaska Constitution, and its repeal unconstitutionally diminished that benefit.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the reinstatement right was not an accrued benefit protected by the constitution, as it was an employment benefit, not a membership benefit, and only applied to active members, not former members, and was merely an offer that could be revoked.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the superior court's summary judgment order, ruling that the statutory reinstatement right was an accrued benefit protected by the constitution and its repeal was unconstitutional.
